newsitem.title: USA: Japanese suspect in embassy attack brought to U.S.
newsitem.headline: Japanese suspect in embassy attack brought to U.S.

text.p: A suspected Japanese extremist was brought to the United States on Monday to face charges in connection with a 1986 mortar attack on the U.S. embassy in Indonesia, the Justice Department said.

It said Tsutomu Shirosaki, 48, had been indicted by a federal grand jury in 1990 for attempting to kill U.S. Embassy personnel by launching two explosive projectiles at the embassy in Jakarta. Nobody was injured in the attack.

The five-count indictment charged him with assault with intent to murder individuals on the embassy gounds, attempted murder, maliciously attempting to harm a U.S. embassy and committing a violent attack against U.S. government personnel.
The criminal charges were unsealed on Monday.
A Justice Department spokeswoman declined to identify the foreign country from which Shirosaki had been brought or to give details of his apprehension.

Other department officials said Shirosaki belonged to the Japanese Red Army, a violent urban guerrilla group, and began serving a 10-year term for armed bank robbery in 1971 in Tokyo but was released in 1977.
The charges in the embassy attack carry a maximum penalty of 30 years in prison.
White House and Justice Department officials hailed the apprehension.

"That's the kind of you-can-run-but-you-can't-hide policy, -- zero tolerance for terrorism -- that the president will be talking about" in a United Nations speech on Tuesday, Richard Clarke, an official of the White House National Security Council, said.

"The United States will not tolerate any act of terrorism, especially senseless acts of violence that put our American men and women abroad in danger," Attorney General Janet Reno said in a statement.
